#6372. A 3-Million-Year-Old Fossil Is Turning the Story of Human Evolution Upside Down

Nearly 3 million years after the Taung Child lived, its fossil is challenging long-held assumptions about humanity’s origins, suggesting our ancient family tree was far more diverse than scientists once believed.

A century ago, a child’s fossil helped establish Africa as the birthplace of humanity. Now, that same discovery is raising another question about our origins: How many early human species have scientists been treating as one?

Discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child became the defining fossil, or “type specimen,” of Australopithecus africanus. It provided the first concrete evidence of human origins in Africa. Yet because no definitive criteria were established for classifying later discoveries, the Taung Child remains the only fossil conclusively assigned to the species.

A new study published in Nature dates the fossil to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and suggests that several supposed members of its species may have belonged to different branches of the human family tree.

Led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), an international team examined tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development during growth.

Several adult fossils traditionally classified as Australopithecus africanus did not match the Taung Child’s developmental trajectory. Differences in brain development were particularly revealing, suggesting that multiple hominin species may have occupied South Africa’s Sterkfontein region, either alongside one another or at different times.

“For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era,” says Professor Gabriele Macho. “Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn’t a neat, straight trunk—it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.”

The environment in which these ancient human relatives lived may help explain their diversity. Fossilized pollen indicates that the Taung Child inhabited a much wetter, more forested landscape than modern South Africa. Some of the trees growing there are now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast.

Over millions of years, alternating wet and dry periods repeatedly transformed the region. As forests and other habitats expanded or contracted, hominin populations may have become isolated, evolved separately, and later encountered one another again. The researchers suggest these shifting conditions encouraged interbreeding and adaptations to different predators and pathogens.

Southern Africa’s position between tropical and temperate ecosystems made it a potential meeting ground for populations that had followed different evolutionary paths.

Rather than a straightforward progression from one ancestor to the next, the findings suggest that the emergence of our genus, Homo, involved a complex network of ancient populations repeatedly separated and reunited by a changing climate.

Reference: “The Taung child and the biogeographic and palaeoclimatic drivers of southern African hominin diversity” by Gabriele A. Macho, Simon Neubauer, Clement Zanolli, Pieter Vermeesch, Kevin L. Kuykendall, Andreas Koutsodendris, Laurin S. Kolb and Thibaut Caley, 5 November 2026, npj Palaeoecosystems. DOI: 10.1038/s44513-026-00008-2

#6371. The Chandra X-Ray Observatory Unmasks a Supernova Impostor

When is an apparent supernova not really a supernova at all? That's a tough question to answer, especially since no supernovae have been observed in the Milky Way in the telescope era. The ones that astronomers see are mostly many millions of light years away in distant galaxies.

SN 1987A was the closest modern supernova, but it exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is still more than 160,000 light years away. And that was before the Hubble launched, and studying its aftermath was difficult. Now we have automated supernova surveys that scan the sky for exploding stars. One such survey detected what seemed to be a supernovae in 2016, in a distant galaxy.

Sometimes, a star exhibits variations in brightness before it explodes as supernovae, and that can create confusion around what's actually happening. That describes the object detected in 2016.

That object was a massive star in a distant galaxy that's showing behaviour associated with a typical supernova explosion. Supernovae explosions are the final act of massive stars that reach the end of their lives, and their prodigious energy output can light up the sky. That's what this star does, sort of.

But unlike a supernova with a single explosion, this star has a volatile outburst every 113 days, something that no supernova can repeat. In an effort to understand what's behind these repeated outbursts, astronomers turned to one of NASA's workhorse space telescopes, the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Chandra's exceptional angular resolution sets it apart from other x-ray observatories, and it can pick out faint sources in detail at great distances.

The volatile star, named AT 2016blu, has about 33 solar masses and is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, around 30 million light years away. AT stands for astronomical transient, and blu is a sequential suffix that tells us the star was the 1,685th transient reported in the year 2016. AT 2016blu is also called a luminous blue variable (LBV), and was first discovered in 2012 by an automated supernova search.

LBVs are rare, and as noted above, exhibit powerful variations in both their brightness and their spectra. Their variability is usually considered to be unpredictable, but in this case, it's periodic.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal has an explanation for AT 2016blu. It's titled "AT 2016blu: Accretion-powered Outbursts in a Luminous Blue Variable and Compact Object Binary," and the lead author is Mojgan Aghakhanloo, a Virginia Institute of Theoretical Astronomy Origins Fellow at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

"We present the first X-ray detection of the supernova (SN) impostor AT 2016blu in NGC 4559," the authors write.

Astronomers are calling AT 2016blu a 'supernova impostor' because LBVs are often detected in supernova searches. "Supernova (SN) impostors are transient events associated with massive stars that are often initially discovered in SN surveys," the authors explain. "However, because their outbursts are less energetic and less luminous than true SNe, and because the star is expected to survive, they are subsequently classified as SN impostors."

Unlike a supernove, AT 2016blu appears to have a nearby companion that triggers the outbursts.

"AT 2016blu exhibited 27 detected quasiperiodic (â¼113 day) outbursts between 2012 and 2026 June, presumably triggered by periastron passages in an eccentric binary system in which the primary is a â³33 Mâ luminous blue variable (LBV)," the authors explain.

Chandra had observed AT 2016blu by accident in 2001-2002, but that was before its first documented outburst. Those observations were actually aimed at another nearby ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX), NGC 4559 X7. XMM-Newton, an ESA x-ray observatory, also observed AT 2016blu four times while looking at NGC 4559 X7. So there's a collection of happenstance observations of the region.

âFor 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis,â said lead author Aghakhanloo. âUntil we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldnât figure out what was making this happen.â

Overall, astronomers observed 27 outbursts of optical light from the supernova impostor between 2012 and 2026. That's one burst about every 113 days, something no supernova can do, since they're destroyed in their explosive outbursts.

âThis starâs behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly itâs not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year,â said co-author NÃºria Torres-AlbÃ , also of the University of Virginia. âTo understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized we needed X-ray data that was timed so that weâd observe the star when it was in an outburst.â

Once it was known to exhibit outbursts, the researchers watched it in optical light leading up to its next predicted outburst. Then they used Chandra to observe it in x-rays, since it's the only x-ray telescope powerful enough to discern AT 2016blu from the other nearby x-ray source, ULX NGC 4559 X7, which is much brighter than the supernova impostor. "We monitored the sourceâs visual-wavelength variability around its predicted outburst time and triggered a Chandra Target of Opportunity (ToO) program in 2026 March, obtaining observations with detections over five closely spaced epochs," the authors write.

The left panel shows a stacked Chandra image of all five target-of-opportunity observations taken during the 2026 March optical outburst of AT 2016blu, in a span of 4 days. The right panel is an XMM-Newton image of the same sky region. XMM-Newton is not as powerful as Chandra, and cannot resolve the two sources. The image is dominated by ULX NGC 4559 X7, much brighter than AT 2016blu. Image Credit: Mojgan Aghakhanloo et al 2026 ApJ 1011 252

âWe suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays,â said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. âThe dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical. So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst.â

Chandra's x-ray data from its 2026 outburst shows that AT 2016blu is 100 times brighter in x-rays than in its data from 2001 to 2002. This is best explained by a binary companion. "These outbursts are most likely triggered by periastron encounters in an eccentric binary system in which the primary is an LBV," the authors write. The secondary is almost certainly a neutron star or a black hole. As they orbit each other, the LBV ejects material that finds its way to the secondary. The material orbits the secondary at very high speeds in an accretion ring, and that heats it up until it emits x-rays.

Based on the x-ray luminosity, the researchers estimate that about 2.7% of Earth's mass is transferred during each outburst.

As is often the case, the researchers had to rule out a potential background source, and for that they relied on Chandra, too. "The alternative to a genuine counterpart to AT 2016blu would be a background quasar with a coincident position," the researchers explain. "This quasar, furthermore, would have brightened at a time coincident with our observations, and thus the AT 2016blu outburst."

These panels are all Chandra images. The first five are from Chandra's observations of AT 2016blu during the ToO campaign, and it's clearly visible during its outbursts. The sixth panel is a stacked image of the region outside of an outburst, clearly showing no background quasar. "No source is detected in the stacked archival images prior to the first observed optical outburst of AT 2016blu, when it was a stable system," the researchers explain. Image Credit: Mojgan Aghakhanloo et al 2026 ApJ 1011 252

"AT 2016blu represents the first observationally known LBV system with a compact companion," the authors write. "Previously studied LBVs either lack X-ray detections or show luminosities consistent with windâwind collisions in massive-star binaries."

Its discovery could shed light on other, similar transient phenomena. Many stars show changes in brightness before they explode as supernovae, and maybe some of them are similar to AT 2016bu. "The discovery of an LBVâcompact-object binary undergoing accretion-powered outbursts also connects AT 2016blu to a growing class of models in which massive starâcompact object binaries explain a variety of pre-SN transient phenomena," the authors explain.

The next step, as is often the case in observations of new types of astrophysical objects, is to find more of them.

"Expanding the sample of such systems is therefore essential to better understand the evolutionary pathways and physical mechanisms connecting SN impostors, LBVs, and interacting SNe," the researchers conclude.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6368. Asteroid Mining Will Crash the Platinum Market, But That’s Good News for Earth

Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question - what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

Platinum Group Metals, or PGMs, are absolutely critical to modern industry. Two of the most commonly used are platinum and palladium, which are critical components in everything from automotive catalytic converters (hence when thereâs a raft of people stealing them) to hydrogen fuel cells. However, these materials are exceptionally hard to come by - on Earth at least. More than 80% of the known planetary reserves are locked in deep-shaft mines located in South Africa and Russia.

Their absurd prices (tens of millions of dollars a ton) are based at least in part on how difficult they are to extract. Even at the Russian and South African mines, they are only able to glean a few grams of material per ton of rock. In the process, they require ventilation, cooling, and heavy machinery, as well as actual laborers down deep mine shafts. That sounds exactly like the kind of industry that is ripe for disruption - at least if there is another source of the raw material.

Fraser talks about whether we will mine asteroids.

Luckily, there is. Metallic (M-type) asteroids are the leftover metallic cores of protoplanets, and carry concentrations of PGMs dozens of times higher than even the richest mines on Earth. A single kilometer-wide space rock of this type holds more PGMs than humans have extracted throughout all recorded history. No wonder these particular materials have been the focus on asteroid mining efforts for decades.

AstroForge, a start-up based in California, is one of a second-round of asteroid mining start-ups that are focusing specifically on returning PGMs to Earthâs market. Instead of multi-billion dollar asteroid mining craft, they specialize in small, agile probes that cost only a few million dollars each to launch. The value of what they return, though, is much higher.

Their architecture involves latching on to the metallic asteroid using magnets. High power lasers then vaporize the asteroidâs crust, and an onboard refinery separates the PGM gas from the less valuable nickel and iron that makes up the majority of the asteroidâs bulk. After the PGMs have been refined, they are blasted back to Earth in a heat-shielded return capsule, ready to be brought to market on Earth itself. That way, the company only ships high value material rather than processing minerals that donât have as much value back down on Earth.

Isaac Arthur is much more bullish on our eventual ability to mine asteroids, as he discusses in this video. Credit - Isaac Arthur YouTube Channel

Understanding how this would affect the terrestrial market is the focus of the paper, and researchers Robert Nachtrieb and Steven Smith built a dynamic computer simulation tracking what they believe will happen to the PGM market over a 20 year period following the first successful return of a chunk of material from an asteroid. According to their model, there will be a dramatic, two-phase transition.

The first phase can be thought of as a âspace gold rushâ. The prices for PGMs have been held artificially high by lack of supply - a classic problem in traditional economics. Once the supplied amount changes - such as when new sources come online, the price begins to fall as the supply line of the classic âXâ graph moves to the right. But it doesnât happen overnight. At the start, space-based metals will be able to be sold at normal prices, allowing the asteroid mining companies to enjoy astronomical profit margins.

Those profit margins will, at least in theory, drive plenty of additional private investment, which in turn will be used to expand the production capacity of the space-based options. According to the paper, this will drive a cycle where industry profits will skyrocket to eight times what they currently are during this first phase. Thatâs enough to make whoever successfully send material back first fabulously wealthy.

But eventually, the second act will begin - what the authors describe as equilibrium collapse. Global supply of PGMs will far exceed original terrestrial amounts, and the market prices will start falling dramatically. High cost mines, such as those operating in North America, will be the first casualties. The Russian and South African behemoths, though, will not be far behind, as they will be unable to maintain a profit with the lower price caused by the increased supply. Over the course of fifteen years, terrestrial mining supplies will be completely replaced by space-mined ones, and market prices will drop by over 75%.

That might sound like terrible news for the terrestrial mining industry - and to put it bluntly, it is. But itâs great news for everyone else. Cheaper PGMs mean less expensive hydrogen electrolyzers, and therefore a less expensive transition to the âgreen economyâ for the rest of the world. In addition, space-based mining does not have all the acid mine drainage, arsenic pollution, and hazardous labor in deep tunnels that are required to get PGMs out of the ground on Earth.

Which all sounds like a much better future for humanity more generally. The problem is the engineering challenges to get to that point. Astroforge has had a few high-profile failures during its development cycle so far. But thatâs the case with any fast-moving ânew spaceâ company. It is undeniably getting closer to making this future world of green tech provided by space rocks a reality. And, if they do manage to do so, everyone involved should become extremely wealthy in a span of less than two decades.

#6367. Archaeologists Uncover 3,800-Year-Old Burial Mystery on Spain’s Coast

A burial ground on Spain’s southern coast suggests ancient communities may have continued building massive shared tombs during the Bronze Age, rather than simply reusing older monuments.

A 3,800-year-old burial mystery on Spain’s southern coast is challenging what archaeologists thought they knew about prehistoric burial traditions.

At a time when communities across the Iberian Peninsula were abandoning massive communal tombs in favor of smaller, individual graves, people near the Strait of Gibraltar appear to have continued burying their dead together. Even more puzzling, the stone monuments they used may have been newly constructed rather than inherited from earlier generations.

The discovery comes from the Trafalgar necropolis, where archaeologists investigated two collective tombs containing the remains of multiple individuals.

Radiocarbon dating of 16 individuals places the use of these tombs between 1875 and 1625 BC, making them among the latest known examples of collective megalithic burial in Iberia.

But the age of the human remains is only part of the mystery. Archaeologists also found no evidence of earlier occupation at the site, raising the possibility that the monuments themselves were constructed during the Bronze Age, when such building traditions were thought to be fading.

The study, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz in Spain and colleagues.

Determining when a tomb was used is not the same as establishing when it was built. Elsewhere in Iberia, Bronze Age communities sometimes buried their dead inside monuments dating back to the Copper Age, making it difficult to distinguish new construction from the reuse of older structures.

Trafalgar may represent an important exception. The absence of evidence for an earlier burial ground suggests the cemetery could have been established in the early second millennium BC. However, additional dating methods are needed to determine when the monuments were originally constructed.

The authors explain, “The Trafalgar megalithic necropolis has revealed a highly significant finding. During the Bronze Age, an entirely new funerary space was constructed in a landscape dominated by the sea. We propose this hypothesis based on the absence of archaeological evidence for earlier occupation in the surrounding area. Until now, the evidence available for this period has primarily pointed to the reuse of megalithic monuments built during the Copper Age. This discovery offers a new perspective on funerary practices during this period and would demonstrate that new monumental burial spaces continued to be constructed.”

The excavations also uncovered grave goods, including gold and copper earrings, silver beads, and an ivory comb, offering additional clues about the people buried at the site.

If further research confirms that the monuments were newly built during the Bronze Age, Trafalgar would provide rare evidence that monumental communal burial traditions survived longer than previously recognized.

Researchers believe additional tombs may remain undiscovered, potentially offering further insight into ancient Iberian burial traditions. However, strong coastal winds and shifting sands threaten to bury the site beneath the dunes again, making continued preservation essential for future excavations.

Reference: “The last builders of megaliths in the South of the Iberian peninsula? The Bronze Age necropolis of Trafalgar (Barbate, Cádiz, Spain)” by Eduardo Vijande-Vila, Serafín Becerra-Martín, Berta Morell-Rovira, Marta Díaz-Zorita Bonilla, Eduardo Molina-Piernas, Alejandro Muñoz-Muñoz, Adolfo Moreno-Márquez, Pablo González-Fernández, Salvador Domínguez-Bella, María Leticia Gómez-Sánchez, Diego Salvador Fernández-Sánchez, José Luis Ramírez-Amador, José María Corona-Borrego, María Carmona-Gil, Jesús Corrales Díaz and Juan Jesús Cantillo-Duarte, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. #6366. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6364. A Strange Liquid Is Helping Scientists Overcome a Major Barrier in Nanotechnology

By filling the tiny pores of fragile materials with an unusual liquid, scientists have found a way to create intricate patterns without destroying their structures.

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) contain networks of tiny pores that can trap gases, capture pollutants, and support chemical reactions. These properties make them attractive for advanced sensors and electronic devices, but their fragile structures are easily damaged by the processes used to manufacture such devices. Researchers in Japan have now developed a way to carve precise patterns into these materials at room temperature without causing the extensive structural damage normally associated with the process.

The technique, developed at Tokyo University of Science (TUS), involves filling the pores of MOFs with an ionic liquid before exposing them to a focused ion beam. In experiments, the liquid strengthened a copper-based MOF and substantially reduced damage, allowing researchers to produce intricate features only a few hundred nanometers wide.

The origins of MOFs trace back to 1974, when University of Melbourne chemistry professor Richard Robson began exploring whether molecules and chemical bonds could replace the wooden balls and metal rods used in structural models. His experiments with copper ions connected by four-armed organic molecules helped establish the foundations of a new class of porous materials. Today, approximately 100,000 MOFs are known, with potential applications ranging from gas storage and chemical separation to pollution control.

Turning these materials into functional devices requires precise fabrication, often involving dry etching, which removes material using energetic particles such as ions. Unfortunately, ion beams can disrupt the delicate crystalline frameworks and produce unwanted cavities. Cryogenic etching has offered a way to limit this damage, but it requires specialized cooling equipment and liquid nitrogen.

Led by Assistant Professor Yumeng Zheng and Professor Kentaro Kinoshita from TUS’s Department of Applied Physics, the researchers investigated whether ionic liquids could make MOFs more resistant to ion beam damage. Their approach builds on earlier findings from Kinoshita’s team showing that these liquids can improve the mechanical stability of MOFs. The study was scheduled for publication in Communications Materials.

The team tested four imidazolium-based ionic liquids in Cu3BTC2, a copper-based MOF containing benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (BTC). Each liquid occupied approximately 50% to 60% of the material’s pore volume. The researchers then used a focused gallium ion beam to etch patterns into the samples at room temperature.

Untreated MOFs suffered substantial structural damage, including the formation of large cavities. Samples containing ionic liquids showed considerably less visible microstructural damage under the same conditions. The researchers successfully etched a square measuring 5 × 5 micrometers (approximately 0.0002 × 0.0002 inches), a pillar, and a Chinese character with lines just 130 to 300 nanometers (about 5 to 12 millionths of an inch) wide.

“In this study, we developed a simple method for room-temperature dry etching of this fragile class of materials. By infiltrating MOFs with ionic liquids, their mechanical stability is greatly improved, and the damage from electron and ion beams is reduced, achieving harmless ion beam etching,” says Dr. Zheng.

The researchers propose that ionic liquids protect MOFs through a combination of thermal and electrical effects. The liquids may absorb heat generated during ion bombardment, reducing local temperature changes, while their mobile ions could help redistribute accumulated electrical charge and screen local electric fields. These mechanisms remain proposed explanations rather than directly established causes of the reduced damage.

Additional measurements confirmed that all four ionic liquid treatments increased the MOF’s hardness without substantially changing its stiffness. Thermal analysis also showed that treated samples decomposed at higher temperatures than untreated material, indicating improved thermal stability.

Although the experiments focused on a single copper-based MOF, the researchers believe the approach could potentially work with other frameworks. If its effectiveness extends to additional materials, room-temperature etching could provide a more accessible route to manufacturing MOF-based devices without the cooling requirements of cryogenic processing.

“We can foresee applications in high-sensitivity sensors, separation and analysis devices, and catalytic devices. This technology has the potential to become a foundational technology for bridging the exceptional material functionalities of MOFs with their use in practical devices,” says Prof. Kinoshita.

Reference: “Ionic-liquid-assisted room-temperature dry etching of metal–organic frameworks” by Yumeng Zheng, Momoka Muraoka, Koki Egawa and Kentaro Kinoshita, 10 November 2026, Communications Materials. DOI: 10.1038/s43246-026-01396-3

This work was partly supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 26K00987.

#6363. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6362. Powerful New Weight-Loss Drug Could Change How Millions Treat Painful Knee Arthritis

An experimental weight-loss injection may offer more than a way to shed pounds, with clinical trials suggesting it could also ease the burden of painful knee arthritis.

Losing weight can help relieve knee osteoarthritis, yet the condition often makes weight loss difficult in the first place. When walking, climbing stairs, or simply standing up from a chair causes pain, getting enough exercise can become a challenge.

For the roughly 15 million Americans living with painful knee osteoarthritis, treatment options remain limited. Physical therapy, topical medications, anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren, opioids, and corticosteroid injections can help manage symptoms, although steroid injections typically provide only short-term relief.

Previous research has shown that losing just 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can improve symptoms. Losing more than 10%, however, is difficult through lifestyle changes alone, particularly for people whose knees already limit their movement.

An experimental weight-loss injection called retatrutide may offer another way to address this problem. In two large clinical trials led by Northwestern University, participants who were overweight or had obesity experienced substantial weight loss alongside significant reductions in knee pain.

The phase 3 trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, involved more than 1,000 participants combined. Those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost approximately 25% of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that about two-thirds of participants receiving the drug reported at least a 50% reduction in knee pain, compared with 38% of those given a placebo.

Researchers tracked these changes using the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC), which asks patients to rate their pain from 0 to 10. Participants also recorded their daily pain levels through an app.

“The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you’re going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain,” said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “A major factor is that you’re loading your knees less and therefore, there’s less pain and it allows you to increase your function.”

Developed by Eli Lilly, retatrutide is a once-weekly injection that activates receptors for three naturally occurring hormones involved in metabolism. Existing weight-loss medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide target one or two receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%. Retatrutide produced losses of approximately 20% to 25% in these trials.

“Participants had remarkable responses,” Schnitzer said. “Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.”

The improvements also extended beyond body weight and joint pain. Participants experienced lower blood pressure, reduced blood lipid levels, and less systemic inflammation, suggesting broader metabolic benefits.

Scientists from Eli Lilly were among the study’s co-authors. Philip Conaghan, professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from the TRIUMPH-4 trial at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were presented separately during a poster session.

Despite the promising results, retatrutide remains experimental and would require approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before becoming a treatment option. Schnitzer emphasized that diet, exercise, and lifestyle changes should remain the first approach because they are less expensive and avoid potential side effects associated with GLP-1 medications, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss. Preserving muscle is especially important for patients with knee osteoarthritis because it helps stabilize the joint.

The trials also left a crucial question unanswered. Although retatrutide significantly reduced pain, researchers do not yet know whether it slows the underlying progression of osteoarthritis or could help patients avoid knee replacement surgery. People who already needed knee replacements were excluded from the studies.

“That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people’s pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis,” Schnitzer said.

Further research must also determine whether retatrutide could benefit people with knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight, since they were not included in the trials. Scientists are particularly interested in whether the drug’s potential anti-inflammatory effects contribute to pain relief independently of weight loss.

“These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known,” Schnitzer said. “Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I’ve been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.”

Reference: “Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity” by Thomas J. Schnitzer, David J. Hunter, Philip G. Conaghan, Arya M. Sharma, Sue D. Pedersen, Kaiyi Chen, So Young Park, Nune Makarova, Kathryn Giblin and Tammy Forrester, 7 November 2026, New England Journal of Medicine. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa2610676

Funding for the study was provided by Eli Lilly and Company.

#6361. Astrophysicists Want to Forecast When a Black Hole Launches Its Jets

Black holes are not just objects. Some astrophysicists prefer to call them locations. From this vantage point, they're locations where the Universe's laws of physics are pushed to their extreme limits.

Black holes are gravitational gluttons that draw everything in their vicinity towards them. When another star strays too close, the black hole can strip its gas away. The gas doesn't necessarily disappear over the event horizon and leave our observable Universe. It first gathers in a rapidly rotating accretion disk, where its temperature is raised to extreme levels. Some of this superheated material is ejected in a pair of collimated jets from the black hole's axis of rotation.

These jets are streams of plasma and particles that can reach relativistic speeds. They can have an enormous reach; the largest ones come from supermassive black holes and can extend for millions of parsecs into space. Though astrophysicists have witnessed many of these jets, their exact causes remain uncertain. The extreme gravity, magnetic fields, and temperatures around black holes is all a part of it.

Astrophysical jets shape their surroundings by heating star forming gas and moving it around on a massive scale. Stars form from cool gas, and the energy from jets works directly against that. The jets can also inflate bubbles where gas is too diffuse to collapse and form stars.

This JWST NIRCam image shows the jets coming from Messier 87, one of the most massive galaxies in the local Universe. These jets aren't from an x-ray binary, they're from its central SMBH that has billions of solar masses. It's an example of extreme astrophysical jets and an indicator of the extreme physics at black holes. Image Credit: Jan RÃ¶der, Maciek Wielgus et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics (2025)

Astrophysicists want to be able to predict when these jets are triggered so they can quickly gather follow-up observations, and new research in The Astrophysical Journal has made some progress. It's titled "Jet Forecast: Timing of Discrete Jet Ejections of Stellar-mass Black Holes Anticipated via X-Ray Properties," and the authors are Toshihiro Kawaguchi and Kazutaka Yamaoka. Kawaguchi is from the Graduate School of Science and Engineering at the University of Toyama, and Yamaoka is from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

The pair of researchers have been working on this problem for a while. In a 2025 study, they examined an x-ray binary consisting of a black hole and a donor star and found a link between the parameters of the inner accretion disk and jet activity. That research suggested that as the accretion disk's inner edge shrank towards its innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the black hole launched its jets. "This fact suggests that the jet materials originate from accreting matter from the innermost part of the disk," the authors wrote.

That was progress, but in that paper the researchers pointed out that more observations were needed. "Both X-ray spectral and timing observations are very important to understand the accretion disk states which can change very rapidly. Dense, simultaneous coverage with radio observations are also crucial to understand diskâjet interactions," the authors wrote in the conclusion to their 2025 paper.

This illustration is representative of XTE J1859+226, the system the authors studied in their 2025 paper. It shows a black hole not only drawing material away from the donor star, but also stretching the star into a distorted shape. Image Credit: J. M. Corral-Santana/Corral-Santana et al. 2011 MNRAS

Their 2025 paper was based on observations of a single black hole x-ray binary gathered during an outburst in 1999â2000. This work is based on observations of four black hole binary systems: one from the 2025 paper and three new ones.

There seem to be changes in an x-ray binary's (XRB) x-ray emissions prior to jets being launched. The spectrum is altered, and variability decreases. Astrophysicists have interpreted these changes as a signal that jets are about to be emitted. But the signals haven't been clear and reliable enough, so astrophysicists haven't been able to use them to time their follow-up observations. The researchers' previous work showed that as an accretion disk's inner edge shrank down to its ISCO, jets were launched. This could be the reliable signal astrophysicists are searching for.

This work expands their observations to more XRBs to see if this holds true. The researchers hope to develop a forecasting model for XRB jet launching so that more complete observations can be obtained.

The results show that the rapidly decreasing radius of the inner disk, called Rin, combined with a decrease in x-ray emission variability (indicated by rms), are a reliable predictor of jet launching. "All the four sources turned out to show the precursors of jet ejections (drops in Rin and rms) 1â10 days before radio activities," the authors write.

This artistâs depiction of a jet ejection shows how the jet from the black hole turns on when the inner radius of the accretion disk shrinks down to the ISCO fast enough. Image Credit: Professor Toshihiro Kawaguchi from University of Toyama, Japan and Dr. Kazutaka Yamaoka from Nagoya University, Japan.

They also found that there are no reliably detected increases in the amount of mass accreted prior to the launching of jets. "They show no huge jumps in M prior to each jet ejection," the researchers explain.

In at least one of the XRBs, that rate actually decayed in the 30 days leading up to jet launching. "We examined the time evolution of the accretion rate M of XTE J1859. It turned out to be exponentially decaying during the outburst (with an e-folding timescale of â¼30 days), and shows no huge jumps around the jet ejections," they write.

But XTE J1859 did show a tantalizing hint of enhancement. "There is a hint of â¼20% enhancement in M just before the jet productions," the authors write.

But that's just a hint, and better observations are needed to support it. "Such fine structures in the time evolution of M will be examined by the better data via the âjet forecastâ in the future," the researchers write.

Another notable finding concerns the Eddington limit. It's a theoretical threshold balanced between the inward force of gravity and the outward force of radiation. In two of the four systems, jets formed below this threshold. Some models of jet ejection say that super-Eddington accretion beyond this limit is necessary to launch jets, but these results say otherwise.

âMonitoring of Rin seems to be suitable for predicting the timing of jet ejections,â said Prof. Kawaguchi. âThe development of a âjet forecastâ would enable us to concentrate observing facilities on the expected timing of jet ejections, thereby accelerating our understanding of jet physics.â

Their jet forecasting model would be based on shrinking Rin and X-ray variability, and when both are detected, alerts would be sent out to other telescopes for more complete observations. Those observation would hopefully reveal some more of the extreme physics that dominate and define black holes.

"When both Rin and rms continuously decrease and when Rin is about to reach the ISCO, alerts can be circulated as a âjet forecastâ for triggering ToO (Target of Opportunity) observations," the authors write.

This is more than just purely academic. Earth has been subjected to bombardment by high-energy particles throughout its history. The Earth's protective magnetic shield deflects most of them, but some get through and trigger showers of secondary particles. Convincing evidence is thin, but some researchers still consider them a factor in the course of life on Earth.

âJet ejections in the Universe produce high-energy photons and particles, such as neutrinos, and such cosmic rays have long influenced the evolution of living creatures on Earth, including human beings,â concluded Prof. Kawaguchi.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

#6359. Scientists Discover a Surprising New Power of Honey That Could Protect Your Skin

Honey’s medical uses may go beyond healing wounds, as laboratory experiments suggest multifloral honey could strengthen human skin cells’ defenses against damaging UV radiation.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight can accelerate skin aging and place cells under stress, potentially contributing to damage that precedes skin cancer. As scientists explore ways to better protect the skin, researchers in Italy are investigating whether multifloral honey could help human skin cells withstand UV exposure.

Honey is already valued in medicine and cosmetics for its antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and wound-healing properties. Sterile honey-based dressings, gels, and ointments are used to treat burns and difficult-to-heal wounds.

Dr. Fikiye Fulya Kavak, a member of Professor Margherita Maioli’s research team at the University of Sassari, Italy, drew inspiration from her background in medical biology and interests in beekeeping and cosmetic science.

“I have always been interested in the fact that certain honeys, such as Manuka honey, are used in medical-grade applications,” Kavak said. “This led me to ask whether high-quality multifloral honey could also show measurable protective effects for human skin cells.”

To investigate, the researchers grew human skin stem cells, fibroblasts, and keratinocytes together in a continuously flowing bioreactor designed to simulate conditions in human skin. Some cultures received a 1% multifloral honey treatment for 48 hours before UV exposure, while others remained untreated.

The team then compared how the cells responded to UV-induced stress. Using real-time quantitative PCR, they also measured the activity of selected genes involved in aging, stress responses, tissue renewal, and stemness, the ability of stem cells to reproduce themselves or develop into specialized cells.

The results suggested that honey pretreatment helped skin stem cells and fibroblasts regulate their responses to UV damage. “In skin stem cells, honey increased the expression of stemness-related markers, while reducing the expression of aging-associated genes,” Kavak said.

Honey-treated stem cells also released less nitric oxide and showed greater antioxidant capacity, suggesting improved defenses against UV-induced stress. Genetic analysis further revealed increased expression of stress-protection genes and changes in signals controlling cell proliferation and renewal.

“What was particularly interesting was that honey seemed to help the cells find a healthier balance after UV stress,” Kavak said. “Rather than pushing the cells into an exaggerated repair response, it appeared to support protective mechanisms while keeping renewal-related signals under control.”

The findings offer an early indication that multifloral honey could support skin protection, although the researchers have not established whether these effects occur in people.

“Our study was performed in cell-based experimental models, not in humans, so further laboratory, preclinical, and clinical studies are needed before any practical recommendation can be made,” Kavak said. Honey should therefore not be considered an alternative to sunscreen.

The team is now investigating the molecular mechanisms behind these responses. “We have been working on protein-level validation studies to confirm whether the molecular changes observed at the mRNA level are also reflected at the protein level,” Kavak said.

Researchers are also exploring a nanofiber-based system that could eventually deliver honey’s active compounds in a controlled, skin-compatible form for cosmetic or medical applications.

“These nanofibers have already been characterized, and their biological evaluation is currently ongoing,” Kavak said. “This represents an important next step, as nanofiber-based systems may provide a more advanced platform for studying the potential skin-related applications of natural bioactive compounds such as multifloral honey.”
