#6338. What Is Science, Really? Even Scientists Can’t Agree

Even scientists in the same specialty disagree about science’s purpose, a survey finds, raising concerns that AI could automate one narrow approach at others’ expense.

Is science a search for objective truth, an exercise in creative problem-solving, or both? A study published in Royal Society Open Science found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science more than the general public does.

Study leader Marina Dubova, a former Santa Fe Institute postdoctoral researcher, is now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. Working with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu, she surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants evaluated 18 historical descriptions of science, including science as detective work, a search for truth, and a mirror reflecting reality.

Scientists and the public generally agreed that science involves following curiosity and solving mysteries. The public tended to share an idealized picture of science as a reliable way to discover how the world works, placing less emphasis on creativity or uncertainty. That outlook could shape how people judge research and help explain their frustration when scientists cannot give firm answers or revise their conclusions as new evidence emerges.

The public’s views were closer to those of physicists and biologists than to those of researchers in psychology or the social sciences. One possible explanation, Dubova suggests, is that physics and biology feature more prominently in science education. More research is needed to test that connection.

Some scientists emphasized the search for objective truth, while others gave more weight to the judgment and creativity researchers bring to their work. They also disagreed about whether research follows established methods or requires improvisation. Few of the 18 descriptions received scientists’ full support, and they often had reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

“What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield,” says Dubova. She suspects that researchers develop their approaches partly through experience, much as chefs develop different instincts about when to follow a recipe and when to improvise. Those differing conceptions of science could influence which discoveries researchers pursue.

That diversity also raises a question for efforts to automate scientific research. As researchers develop artificial intelligence systems capable of conducting science, whose understanding of the work will those systems embody? Dubova worries that automation could reinforce one narrow conception of science at the expense of other valuable approaches.

For Dubova, the study is an early step toward understanding how these outlooks shape research itself. “Don’t take the common understanding of science for granted,” she says. “Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.”

Reference: “Everyone knows what science is…until you ask” by Marina Dubova and Qiawen E. Liu, 11 November 2026, Royal Society Open Science. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260933

The research was supported by SFI’s Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, established in 2022 to support exploratory research by early-career scientists. Dubova used the funding to compensate study participants, helping make the research possible.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6336. LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date

An international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.

For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.

This new view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.

The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON

"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.

In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This new view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.

The other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.

The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON

According to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.

The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

#6335. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6334. Researchers Have Discovered That a 6,000-Year-Old Clue to Ireland’s Farming History Was Completely Wrong

Protein tests on ancient bones have removed evidence of farming’s influence in Ireland before 4000 BCE, reopening questions about when the island first encountered agriculture.

For more than 30 years, the “Kerry Cow” helped shape a story about how farming reached Ireland. Bone fragments found on the coast of County Kerry appeared to show that domesticated cattle had arrived while the island’s inhabitants still lived by hunting and gathering. A new analysis has revealed that those supposed cattle were a bear and a wild boar.

The fragments were unearthed during excavations in the 1980s and 1990s at Ferriter’s Cove, a small bay on the Dingle Peninsula. Dated to the end of Ireland’s Mesolithic period, which lasted from 8000 to 4000 BCE, they were considered the earliest evidence of domesticated farm animals in either Ireland or Britain.

Their identification as cattle challenged existing theories about Ireland’s transition to farming, suggesting that its hunter-gatherers had established links with Neolithic farmers arriving from continental Europe before agriculture took hold on the island.

Researchers led by Dr. Martin Moucheron at University College Dublin (UCD) returned to the original archaeological material, now stored at University College Cork (UCC). Working with Drs. Benjamin Gearey, Barra Ó Donnabháin, and Margaret McCarthy at UCC, and Kate Kanne at UCD, the team sent the bones to the CNRS laboratory in Lille, France.

There, the fragments underwent analysis using ZooMS, a technique that identifies animals through proteins preserved in ancient bone collagen, a structural component of bone. The results identified bear and wild boar rather than the domesticated cattle on which the earlier interpretation depended.

Reported in the latest edition of PAST, the newsletter of the Prehistoric Society, the findings remove a major piece of evidence from debates about when and how communities in Ireland and Britain moved from hunting and gathering to farming. There is currently no archaeological evidence supporting the idea that domesticated cattle, and by extension early farming communities, had reached or influenced Ireland before 4000 BCE. Losing that evidence does not establish a new arrival date, but it changes the basis for reconstructing that transition.

“Ferriter’s Cove is an iconic archaeological site, originally excavated by the Late Professor Peter Woodman, Department of Archaeology, UCC; this new collaboration with colleagues at UCD marks an exciting new phase of research and these remarkable results are set to change our understanding of the earliest evidence for agriculture in Ireland,” said Gearey.

The work is part of a Research Ireland-funded postdoctoral project at UCD’s School of Archaeology, led by Moucheron under the mentorship of Professor Graeme Warren. The project is reexamining important Mesolithic archaeological sites using modern scientific techniques.

Warren added, “These exciting results show the real value in going back to key sites with new analytical techniques – which can change the stories we tell about our past”

“For at least four millennia hunting and gathering people lived on the island, and there is a common conception that they left little trace and that we know very little about them – unlike the megaliths of Neolithic farmers, who are portrayed in ways that feel very familiar in Ireland,” said Moucheron.

“But there is much we can understand about Mesolithic people just by going back to the sites and material we have, and by looking at them with new eyes and new techniques – and an open mind.”

Further analyses are underway to determine whether the bear remains belonged to brown bears or polar bears. The researchers hope this work will provide new insights into Ireland’s prehistoric bear populations before their extinction during the Bronze Age.

Reference: “No sacred cows: ZooMS identification of the Late Mesolithic bone assemblage at Ferriter’s Cove, Co. Kerry, Ireland”.

#6333. SpaceX Launches Starship But Passes Up Booster Catch for Safety's Sake

SpaceX sent its Starship on a flight that was meant to feature a first-ever retrieval of both rocket stages, but a launch-pad catch of the first-stage booster had to be canceled due to safety concerns.

Instead, the Super Heavy booster was diverted during its descent to make an offshore splashdown. Observers at SpaceX's Starbase on the South Texas coast could hear the sonic boom and see the fiery plunge that took place minutes after launch at 4:47 p.m. CT (2247 GMT) today. "Wow, you could feel the rumble of that splashdown there," launch commentator Jessie Anderson said.

This 15th flight test still has a chance to make history: The mission plan calls for the Starship second stage to spend as much as 22 hours in orbit â ending with a return to the pad for a midair capture by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms. SpaceX has caught Starship's booster during three previous test flights, but this would be a first for a second stage.

Hours after launch, SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice said the booster's control system triggered an abort of the launch-tower catch because the boostback engine burn ended early, apparently due to a low fuel mass alarm. SpaceX's team was still troubleshooting the root cause of the alarm, she said.

Anderson said the offshore splashdown averted the risk of damage or injuries at the launch site. "Safety is always our No. 1 priority," she said. If any further safety concerns arise, SpaceX's mission team has the option of ending the flight early and sending the second stage â known as Ship 42 â down to a controlled ocean splashdown.

After reaching orbit, Ship 42 deployed 26 satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. Three of the satellites were equipped with a suite of cameras to inspect Ship's heatshield after deployment.

Starship ranks as the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, standing 407 feet (124 meters) tall and providing 17 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. The rocket is designed to deploy dozens of Starlink V3 satellites at a time â and eventually send thousands of explorers and settlers to Mars.

NASA is counting on SpaceX to provide a Starship-based system for landing astronauts on the moon by as early as 2028. As a preparatory step, NASA is planning to test Starship as well as Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system in low Earth orbit next year. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman referred to that test mission, known as Artemis III, in a post to X that took note of the video sent down from orbit via the Starlink network.

"Congratulations to the SpaceX team on another spectacular launch," Isaacman wrote. "Very much appreciate how you bring the world along in high resolution. We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III."

This report has been updated with further details about the aborted booster catch.

#6332. The Best 4K TVs Bring Everything You Watch and Play to Life

4K is the standard, and there are so many great options right now.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Now more than ever, you should hold your TV to a higher standard. More and more streaming content is available in 4K UHD resolution, which has four times as many pixels as standard Full HD (1080p). Video games, including PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch 2, support higher refresh rates that only TVs from the past few years support.

4K TVs are the standard, and have been for some time. Technically, 8K TVs are available, but there’s no indication that anyone is making content to take advantage of them anytime soon.

While tech prices are abnormally high in 2026, the tech is still improving rapidly. And since most of us buy a TV every five to 10 years, even last year’s models will offer a huge upgrade and are generally much more reasonably priced. New TVs are out there for everyone, at every price point.

I handpicked 4K TVs based on my testing and included options at various price points from current leading manufacturers: LG, Samsung, Hisense, and TCL. The selection process involved parsing through hardware specs, attending live demo sessions, and consulting with other industry experts.

Unless indicated otherwise, I usually test the 65-inch version of each TV, since it usually offers the best balance of price and capabilities as the primary home entertainment centerpiece in your space. Most sets are also available in smaller, less expensive versions. And many are available in even XXL formats, 75 inches and higher, for households with larger spaces and bigger budgets.

A note on these picks: Even though we’re well into 2026, we still primarily recommend TVs that launched in 2025, even when a newer version is available. From what my colleagues and I have seen so far, I believe that last year’s models represent the best possible value right now. In time, as last year’s models sell out, the value proposition will change. But trust me when I say that these TVs provide the best value and will make your shows, movies, and games look great for years to come.

Now that the price has come down a bit, we’re prepared to recommend this year’s LG C-series TV, the C6 evo, as the best option for most people. Though it isn't dramatically different from its predecessor, this mid-range OLED maintains the line’s legacy as impressively slim, elegant, and capable of delivering a stunning picture. It also runs a feature-packed platform with deep smart home integration.

With millions of individually backlit pixels, the C6’s OLED display is a rock-solid contender for the best in its price range. The panel’s flawless black reproduction delivers perfect contrast and vivid colors, making any content—from a newscast to a blockbuster movie to an AAA video game—look its best.

Speaking of gaming, the C6 is also one of the best TVs on the market for the task. In addition to being a great companion for the latest gaming consoles, the TV can double as a top-tier gaming monitor, thanks to a 165 Hz refresh rate and support for AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync. It can also deliver high-powered cloud-based gameplay via an Nvidia GeForce Now subscription.

As with previous years, the C6 also gets extra credit for its wide size range. Depending on your needs and budget, you can choose a compact 42-inch, a private movie theater-worthy 83-inch model, or one of several additional sizes in between. Keep in mind that larger screen models have brighter Tandem OLED screens.

With a price cut shortly after launch, the TCL QM8L is ready to replace its predecessor, the QM8K, as the top Mini-LED TV. It looks incredibly sleek sans top and side bezels, and the picture looks just as impressive. While OLED technology still broadly produces the richest and sharpest image quality, mini-LED TVs are no slouch, delivering great detail and a brighter screen that improves performance in less-than-stellar lighting conditions.

With thousands of local dimming zones and an upgraded AI-powered processor to control them, the QM8L’s super quantum-dot mini-LED screen delivers a captivating picture with rich colors and deep contrast. The TV’s picture quality comes close to a top-tier OLED TV. Its higher peak brightness and lower cost sufficiently make up for its lack of individually backlit pixels.

If you are looking for a mini-LED 4K TV with SQD color proficiency on a tighter budget, I think this model’s more affordable cousin, the TCL QM7L, is also a very good choice. You lose some peak brightness and local dimming zones, but it still provides amazing performance for its much lower price.

RGB Mini-LED TVs deliver a unique combination of high peak brightness and stellar color accuracy, with the latter made possible by separate red, blue, and green light diodes instead of a single one in their display panels. Of all the TV newcomers to offer this screen technology in 2026, the Hisense UR9 is the one I’d recommend to most buyers. Beyond the exceptional picture quality from its new display panel, the TV also delivers surprisingly powerful sound and a rich set of futureproof connectivity features.

In addition to producing a bright picture with vibrant-yet-accurate colors and deep contrast, the Hisense UR9 surprised me pleasantly by handling direct light reflections surprisingly well. Dubbed “Obsidian” by its maker, the standout glare-reduction feature results in a top-tier viewing experience in bright spaces.

The TV’s screen supports a high 180Hz refresh rate, cutting latency in video games and smoothing blurred movement in live sports. I’m also a big fan of its 4.1.2-channel speaker system tuned by Devialet — a French luxury audio brand — and its two-year warranty.

Consider the Hisense UR8 if you are looking for an RGB Mini-LED TV on a tighter budget. It is a step down in peak brightness and audio performance from the UR9, as its model number suggests, but the lower price makes up for the shortcomings. Unlike its flagship sibling, the UR8 is also available with a 55-inch screen.

TCL’s QM6K is my favorite 4K TV on a budget. Spending less than $600 before additional deals and discounts, gets you a TV with a sleek design, superb picture quality, a feature-packed platform, and an abundant set of connectivity options. With a high-performance game mode and support for variable refresh rate, the TV is also a top-notch gaming console display.

The TCL QM6K delivers superb picture quality and color rendering for a TV at such an agreeable price point. Its quantum-dot mini-LED display panel with hundreds of local dimming zones produces punchy colors and dramatic contrast that defy its price category. I can’t think of a better 4K TV for the money.

On the audio front, the TV is as impressive as it is in terms of picture quality. Its speaker system, tuned by Onkyo, has a built-in subwoofer, allowing it to deliver immersive sound with surprisingly powerful bass.

TCL offers the QM6K in several screen sizes, with the 98-inch model as the largest. The biggest screen size costs a little over $2,000, which is quite a bargain for the full-blown private movie theater experience it provides. The 85-inch version at a tad above $1,000 is also a great value for money.

The Samsung S95H is the 4K TV to get if you want stunning design and picture quality to match. The TV’s metal frame gives it a unique presence, especially when wall-mounted, and makes any rival look generic in comparison. Its super-bright QD-OLED display predictably produces vibrant colors and deep contrast. Plus, a sophisticated onboard processor with access to AI neural networks makes lower-resolution content look sharper than ever.

Most importantly, the Samsung S95H can effortlessly deliver this viewing experience from any angle, even in bright spaces. The TV’s screen has a glare-free finish, which makes it practically impervious to light reflections. This means its picture quality stays superb even when it’s facing a lamp, a window, or another light source. This quality alone makes the TV worth every penny.

In keeping with its price category, the Samsung S95H is also a bona fide gaming powerhouse, capable of delivering exceptional visuals when connected to a gaming console or a high-powered computer. Samsung’s Tizen platform also supports cloud gaming, so all you need is a wireless controller and a monthly subscription to enjoy AAA titles.

We like that the TV’s intuitive remote has a rechargeable battery that you can charge via a light source or a USB-C port, so you never have to swap batteries. Its multi-speaker Dolby Atmos audio system, meanwhile, defies its form factor.

The TCL X11L is the best big-screen TV on the market today, with an elegant design, outstanding picture quality, and immersive sound tuned by Bang & Olufsen. We often think of TCL as the bang for your buck, but this set shows the brand can also deliver something out of this world for folks willing to spend big for the best possible picture.

The secret is the X11L's first-of-its-kind SQD Mini-LED display—that's "Super Quantum Dot"—which blends brightness-enhancing quantum dot technology with Mini-LED dimming zones to boost high-dynamic-range performance.

At a $7,000 launch price, it was hard to imagine not insisting on an OLED TV over the TCL X11L, but things have changed dramatically since then. Now that it starts at $3,000 for a 75-inch version, the high-end TCL offering is a great buy. Its color accuracy and contrast are both top-notch, and the overall picture quality is tremendous. Frankly, I’d take the TV over any OLED on the market today.

TVs that double as home decor pieces by displaying artwork or photos became a thing when Samsung launched The Frame almost a decade ago. Since then, frame-like TVs have grown from a niche category into something with broader appeal and a surprisingly rich selection across the price spectrum. The Hisense S7 CanvasTV is the one I’d recommend to most buyers in 2026, because it strikes a fine balance between elegant design, stellar picture quality, and a rich selection of onboard features, all at a reasonable price and in multiple screen sizes.

Thanks to a quantum-dot display with a matte finish to reduce pesky reflections and an ambient light sensor, the S7 CanvasTV can display beautiful visuals in any scenario, whether it’s live sports or a vacation photo. Still, you should know the device’s picture quality can’t match that of similarly priced conventional Hisense TVs or rival brands with quantum-dot or RGB mini-LED screens. The matte screen, customizable frame, and slim wall mount make the S7 CanvasTV worth considering, since it will look great when not in use.

When it comes to alternatives, the first that comes to mind is Samsung's The Frame Pro. It offers a more polished design and a fancier quantum-dot mini-LED panel with superior glare resistance and artwork display capabilities. The Frame Pro will look much nicer as an art piece, but I’d still take the Hisense S7 CanvasTV for offering Dolby Vision HDR support and a full set of built-in connectivity features. Samsung has these essentials in a separate box for The Frame Pro.

Though they all look like black slabs on the wall, the quality of the images produced by 4K TVs can vary dramatically from model to model. Many also have distinctive features that make them better for specific applications—like a high refresh rate for gaming. And, of course, all that impacts how much they cost. Here are the most important things to keep in mind while shopping:

There is all manner of exotic formulae for determining the exact distance you should sit from a large screen TV—X-times the screen height, X-times the screen’s diagonal size—but there isn’t a right or wrong answer. The best rule of thumb is if the screen fills your frame of vision from where you’re sitting, and you don’t have to turn your head to see one side of the screen or the other, you’re fine. (Note: Sitting too close to a 4K TV won’t ruin your eyes despite what your mother may have told you.)

What size TV you choose, however, may be predetermined by your room geography and/or furnishings, such as the interior of an existing TV cabinet, or dictated by a spouse’s objections to a larger-size set. If you plan to buy a new TV larger than your current set, measure the width, height, and depth of your home’s TV space, and then check the actual width and height of the TV with stand, not the diagonal screen size. A flat panel 65-inch screen 4K TV usually measures less than 60 inches wide, less than 36 inches tall, and about 15 inches deep with the stand.

Building a Home Theater? Check These Guides Next: Best OLED TVs • Best Wireless Surround Sound Systems • Best TV Wall Mounts

Some TVs come with center stands, while many larger models have feet at either end of the set, which may be too widely spaced apart for your TV stand. Check the width of your TV tabletop and the space between the feet of your prospective TV purchase to make sure its feet will fit.

Planning to hang your TV on a wall? All TVs follow a version of the VESA (Video Electronics Standards Association) wall-mounting standard, including variations such as VESA MIS-D, MIS-E, and MIS-F, which mainly address a TV’s rear mounting-hole spacing, supportable weight, and size.

A VESA wall mounting kit can work with virtually any wall-mountable TV, but double-check your TV’s specifications to confirm any VESA variation.

A 4K TV’s display is composed of 3840 x 2160 pixels, but that’s only the screen resolution. A dizzying array of screen technologies creates different levels of stunning 4K images. These technologies include:

A TV screen's image speed is measured by its refresh rate, expressed in hertz (Hz). This equals frames flashed per second; for comparison, movie film is projected at 24 frames per second, while Normal TV broadcasts refresh at 60 Hz, or 60 frames per second.

If you’re a heavy gamer, you want a display that more accurately reflects the eye-blinking speed of the animated action, which means you’ll want a TV with a refresh rate of at least 120 Hz or higher, and a set equipped with VRR (variable refresh rate), which automatically adjusts the refresh rate depending on the content being displayed.

Another screen technology gamers want is low latency, or input lag, which is how quickly the display responds when you push a button on your controller or joystick. Many higher-end TVs include Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), which automatically switches your TV to a faster, more responsive mode measured in milliseconds (ms).

Yes, but you only need to concern yourself with the types your 4K TV includes. Nearly all bigger-screen 4K TVs are equipped with a type of HDR (high-dynamic range) that creates visibly punchier, higher-contrast images when viewing 4K content from Blu-ray or streaming channels.

Different HDR versions include the standard and most common HDR, as well as the more specialized HDR-10, HDR-10+, Dolby Vision, and HLG (Hybrid Log Gamma), designed to deliver HDR benefits to lower non-4K broadcast, cable, and satellite TV fare.

While there are subtle visual benefits associated with each type of HDR, and while some TV makers, 4K Blu-ray producers, and streaming channels opt to deploy some HDR versions but not others, compatibility really isn’t an issue since all include a plain and widely compatible HDR version.

Bottom line: Any set featuring any type of HDR will produce a visibly better 4K picture than a set without HDR.

8K TV makers may not want to hear this, but probably never. 8K TVs offer a display with a resolution of 7,680 x 4,320 pixels, or 33 million pixels, more than four times the 8 million pixels that comprise a 4K TV display.

Prices are coming down to near 4K TV price levels for 8K models. But, for a variety of reasons, there is no existing 8K content—no 8K broadcast or cable, no 8K streaming, no 8K Blu-ray—and there isn’t likely to be for the foreseeable future.

The only benefits of an 8K TV are via upscaling or up-conversion of lower-resolution programming to 8K. But realistically you’ll need at least a 75-inch TV to appreciate the difference between 4K and 8K.

Imagine watching the movie "Jaws" without feeling that "bum-bum, bum-bum" bass in your gut, or not being able to understand character dialogue over a swelling orchestral passage, or subtle sounds that lend a dramatic scene its key ambience.

A 4K TV may produce excellent picture quality, but most do not produce equally excellent sound, which can dull or ruin your viewing experience. There is a fix for this. Instead of relying on a TV’s poor audio, you may want to pair your 4K TV with a soundbar via an ARC (Audio Return Channel) or eARC (enhanced Audio Return Channel) HDMI connection.

An ARC-compatible soundbar connected to a TV via an ARC HDMI jack lets you control your TV’s picture and sound with a single remote, as if the soundbar were your TV’s speaker.

Just make sure to measure the space between your TV tabletop and the bottom of the TV display area so your prospective soundbar won’t block either the screen or the TV’s IR remote control sensor.

#6331. James Webb Telescope Reveals a Giant Planet That Was Hiding in Plain Sight

Finding planets like Earth may depend on better ways to read telescope images, after a new technique uncovered a giant world already captured by JWST.

A giant planet was hiding in observations taken by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), even though astronomers already knew it existed. The telescope had captured its faint light, but the overwhelming glow of its host star made the planet impossible to distinguish using conventional image-processing techniques.

This is one of the biggest challenges in photographing planets beyond our solar system. Stars are extraordinarily bright compared with the worlds orbiting them, and even JWST, which can observe galaxies billions of years in the past, struggles to separate a planet’s faint signal from its star’s glare.

Researchers led by Northwestern University developed a new computational technique that helped overcome this problem. By accounting for tiny imperfections in the telescope, they improved its sensitivity to faint planets by 2 to 15 times and recovered a giant planet that had remained hidden in two-year-old observations. Their findings were published in the journal Nature.

“Planets are a million times fainter than their stars,” said Northwestern’s Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, who led the study. “So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare. That is a very tricky problem because even the tiniest changes in the telescope can affect how that glare appears. Slight shifts or tilts — even on the scale of just a few nanometers — can change the pattern of light. Our method models how light travels through the telescope and accounts for those tiny changes, allowing us to remove the glare much more precisely.”

Ferrer-Chavez is a Ph.D. student in astronomy at Northwestern’s Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and a member of Jason Wang’s research group. Wang, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at Weinberg, co-authored the study. Both researchers belong to Northwestern’s Center for Interdisciplinary Exploration and Research in Astrophysics (CIERA).

Astronomers have long relied on specialized instruments called coronagraphs to block starlight when searching for planets. Even relatively bright young giant planets can be 100,000 times fainter than their stars, making this step essential. However, some light still escapes around the coronagraph, creating patterns of glare that can conceal nearby objects.

“For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference,” Wang said. “Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden.”

The difficulty is that a telescope never remains perfectly still. Minute changes in its mirrors and other components can alter how starlight spreads across an image. Even a slight mismatch between the reference photograph and the original observation can leave enough residual glare to hide a planet.

“We try to make telescopes extremely stable, but there are extreme engineering challenges that we haven’t quite solved yet,” Wang said. “There are known causes of instability and unknown causes. Small thermal changes could cause a mirror to expand or contract by a picometer. Telescopes like JWST have cryocoolers to keep the instrument super cold. Those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. So, there are issues like those but also issues that we still don’t understand as we learn how to build these complex telescopes.”

To address these limitations, the Northwestern researchers developed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Instead of relying entirely on reference photographs, the technique creates a digital twin of the telescope, a computer model that recreates how starlight travels through its mirrors and reaches its detectors.

The team used powerful computational tools to adjust millions of parameters in the model, accounting for subtle movements, optical distortions, and other imperfections. By repeatedly refining the simulation until it closely matched the real observations, FLIP could reproduce the unwanted starlight more accurately and subtract it from the image.

This visualization demonstrates the image processing method, called FLIP, as it subtracts starlight from a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observation of star 51 Eridani A (51 Eri) in the F430M filter. Starlight subtraction proceeds with the iteration number shown in the lower left, eventually revealing the faint planet 51 Eri b at its expected location. Credit: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez

Although the approach used optimization techniques commonly associated with machine learning, it relied on the known physics of the telescope rather than artificial intelligence to recognize planets.

“We used the same computational tools that researchers use to train AI models, but we did not actually use AI,” Wang said. “Because we already know the physics, we don’t need AI to understand what’s happening.”

The researchers tested FLIP using existing JWST observations of three stars. Two, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, had known planets, while the third, TYC 5899, had no known planetary companions. The technique consistently outperformed conventional image processing, particularly when examining light from extremely faint objects.

One of the clearest demonstrations involved 51 Eridani b, a giant planet previously discovered using ground-based telescopes. Although astronomers knew the planet existed, it had remained hidden in JWST observations at an infrared wavelength of 4.3 microns.

That wavelength is especially valuable because carbon dioxide strongly absorbs infrared light there, potentially allowing astronomers to investigate a planet’s atmospheric composition. However, carbon dioxide absorption in 51 Eridani b’s atmosphere made its already faint signal even harder to detect.

When Ferrer-Chavez applied FLIP to the same observations, the planet emerged from the glare.

“We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn’t see,” Wang said. “This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way.”

The result suggested that valuable information about distant planets could already be present in existing telescope observations, waiting for better processing methods to reveal it. More precise removal of starlight could also help astronomers study planets at different wavelengths, potentially uncovering new details about their atmospheres.

The approach could have implications for future space missions as well. NASA’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars. Detecting such small, faint worlds may require optical stability at the picometer scale, equivalent to trillionths of a meter. That would mean keeping the telescope roughly 100 to 1,000 times more stable than JWST.

Rather than relying entirely on engineering to achieve that precision, methods like FLIP could potentially compensate for some of the tiny imperfections that interfere with observations. For now, the researchers hoped their technique would help astronomers recover previously hidden planets and expand the range of worlds they could study.

“We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system,” Ferrer-Chavez said. “It’s not that they don’t exist. It’s that we cannot see them. Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is.”

Reference: “Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit” by Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, Jason J. Wang, Katherine L. Bouman, William T. Freeman, Laurent Pueyo, Brandon Y. Feng and Marshall D. Perrin, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

#6329. Astrophysicists Cross Another Dark Matter Candidate Off Their List: Stupendously Large Black Holes

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.

There are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe. They're hypothetical too, but are massive objects, so their presence should be detectable in a way that particles aren't.

All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different. But PBHs have fairly well-defined search strategies that should detect them if they exist. If they exist, then cosmologists should find evidence of them in the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

The CMB is relic radiation from the Big Bang itself, the oldest detectable light that exists. It was released when the Universe was only about 380,000 years old. For the most part, the CMB appears smooth and uniform, or isotropic. But increasingly powerful detectors let cosmologists examine the CMB for minor fluctuations. Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. Yes, that's two billions one after another.

This is a temperature map of the CMB created with data from the ESA's Planck spacecraft. The CMB can only be measured from space, and Planck's job was to measure anisotropies in the CMB. The different colours show temperature differences, and those differences correspond to where the first galaxies formed. Image Credit: NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=130789180

New research published in Physical Review Letters says that SLABs can't be dark matter. It's titled "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," and the lead author is Christopher Gerlach. Gerlach is a theoretical physicist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and its PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence.

âA possible solution to the puzzle of dark matter was that it might have collected shortly after the Big Bang in giant black holes with masses ranging from 100 million to 10 billion billion times that of the sun," said lead author Gerlatz.

This work is largely based on the ESA's Planck satellite. The Planck satellite ended its mission in 2013, but researchers are still generating new insights from its data. Part of that is because of more raw computing power. But it's also because they can cross-correlate it with new data from sources that didn't exist back in 2013. Physicists also have better ways to filter out interference, like that from the Milky Way.

âThat we are still generating new insights into the universeâs evolution and structure 13 years after it was shut down only emphasizes how important the Planck satellite was and is to physicists," explained Gerlach.

âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â - Nicholas Leister, Johannes Gutenberg University.

SLABs, if they're real, formed from overdensities of matter after the Big Bang. They didn't need to form massive stars, burn their fuel, and explode as supernovae. They skipped that step, and are too massive for that, anyway. Since they're theorized to have formed so early, before massive objects like galaxy clusters, they should be the only things that left such an imprint on the CMB.

âIf these SLABs had existed in large numbers and contained significant amounts of dark matter, they would have left a characteristic imprint on the CMB through their unique perturbations, or, in a word, making it grainy," said study co-author Nicholas Leister, also a JGU physicist.

This image is an artist's interpretation of what primordial black holes could look like. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these. Image Credit: NASA

Previous work has all but eliminated the possibility that regular primordial black holes could account for all dark matter. But what about SLABs? Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins?

To find out, the researchers first modelled SLABs and how they would affect the CMB. Then they compared the modelled effects to the actual CMB. The result was clear: the CMB doesn't have the characteristic graininess that SLABs should have imprinted on it.

"In this work, we have shown that the production of stupendously large PBHs would generate large DM isocurvature perturbations, tightly constrained by CMB and BAO data," the authors explain.

"We show that primordial black holes (PBHs) in the Stupendously Large Black Hole mass range (Mâ³1011Mâ) produce isocurvature perturbations exceeding current Planck Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) limits, thereby excluding them as a significant dark matter component," the authors conclude.

This artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disc. SMBH are massive and they're real. But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. Credit: ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser

The results also counter some other thinking regarding PBHs and dark matter. When the JWST discovered its notorious early massive galaxies, galaxies so massive that they challenged models of galaxy formation, it set the astrophysical community in motion searching for explanations. Astrophysicists cast their net wide, and one explanation they caught concerned PBHs. One 2022 study, titled "Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.

But that's unlikely to be true, according to these results.

"They also challenge scenarios attributing the early massive galaxy candidates observed by James Webb Space Telescope to PBH-induced fluctuations," the researchers write.

SLABs were also potential explanations for another unexplained phenomenon. A gravitational wave background hum pervades the Universe, sensed by Pulsar Timing Arrays, and some researchers asked if SLABs could be responsible. "These questions are also unlikely to be answered by SLABs, since our findings show that they didnât exist in large numbers," said Nicholas Leister. âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â

So the search for dark matter candidates continues. It's possible that no one type of object or particle makes up dark matter. Dark matter may be a collective effect generated by different particles, objects, or phenomena.

But it looks like SLABs are no longer in contention.

#6328. When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

The study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:

Isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

One issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser shows how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Said Eser:

We are not claiming to have discovered a new gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

Further Reading: Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin

#6327. Scientists Uncover a Bizarre Quantum Effect Where Time Could Flow at Different Speeds Simultaneously

Scientists have developed a theoretical framework that could allow atomic clocks to reveal a strange quantum effect in which different flows of time exist simultaneously.

Raise an atomic clock by just a few millimeters, and it ticks slightly faster because gravity is weaker at the higher position. Today’s most precise clocks can detect this tiny difference, confirming a prediction of Einstein’s theory of relativity. But quantum physics introduces a stranger possibility: A single clock could exist in a superposition of different motions, potentially experiencing multiple rates of time simultaneously.

Scientists have now developed a theoretical method to detect the quantum effects of these different flows of time using advanced atomic clocks. Published in Physical Review Letters, the research shows how trapped-ion clocks could reveal a previously unobserved connection between quantum mechanics and relativity. The proposed approach uses existing experimental technology and could bring researchers closer to testing how time behaves in the quantum world.

According to Einstein’s theory of relativity, time passes at different rates depending on an object’s speed and the strength of gravity. Atomic clocks are sensitive enough to detect these differences across height changes of just a few millimeters. They measure time using precise atomic frequencies and are essential to technologies such as GPS.

Quantum mechanics introduces another possibility. An atomic clock’s motion can exist in a superposition of different states, potentially exposing it to multiple rates of time simultaneously. Under these conditions, the clock’s motion becomes entangled with its internal energy, producing changes in its quantum properties that researchers believe can be measured.

“It’s the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock’s motion becomes “entangled” with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques,” explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the study’s lead authors.

The international research team, led by scientists at Kyushu University and working with collaborators in the United States, Canada, and Sweden, also developed a theoretical approach for precisely controlling the motion of trapped ions. This could substantially increase the detectability of the quantum effect.

“We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock’s motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.”

The next challenge is to translate the theoretical framework into an experiment that can reliably detect the predicted quantum signature while accounting for disturbances and uncertainties in real laboratory conditions. If successful, the approach could establish atomic clocks as tools for investigating the quantum behavior of time and potentially improve future clock technology.

“Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model,” concludes Foo. “We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.”

Reference: “Quantum Signatures of Proper Time in Optical Ion Clocks” by Gabriel Sorci, Joshua Foo, Dietrich Leibfried, Christian Sanner and Igor Pikovski, 20 April 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/qhj9-pc2b

Funding: National Science Foundation, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, John Templeton Foundation, Simons Foundation, Banting Postdoctoral Fellowship, Novartis Science Scholarship

The article’s author: “Raise an atomic clock by just a few millimeters, and it ticks slightly faster because gravity is weaker at the higher position.” Agreed, however, it is the clock that speeds-up, not time. Time is just an arbitrary label attached to the observation of the progression of a full spectrum of events to describe their duration. As a lay discoverer and investigator I’ve been demonstrating and writing of the true nature of gravity/time since 2012, with little notice. To the best of my knowledge the problem began with Thomas Young misinterpreting the results of his ‘double-slit’ experiments as a ‘duality of particles and waves.’ That was based on the still misunderstood nature of gravity. In my model of gravity it is externally induced in all matter/objects by some still unidentified higher force to radiate to the extremes of the universe in fields of coherent pulsing angular lines of generally attractive force, in accordance with the well established ‘inverse-square law’ of attraction. I believe I’ve already proved that with four of my own demonstration videos, the most recent of them being (https://odysee.com/@charlesgshaver:d/5Gravity:c). If I’m right, as I’m sure I am, then time flowing at different speeds simultaneously is quite simply not possible.

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

Einstein’s sorrowful silhouette has faded into the distance. But his intuition, his persistence, his belief in “local realism”, has finally found its rightful home in the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT). Einstein was not a failed prophet, but a true physicist misunderstood by his era.

#6326. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.
